history.heading: Ancient North Africa
paragraphs: The land of present-day Algeria has been inhabited for hundreds of thousands of years, and the rock art of the Tassili n'Ajjer in the Sahara records life there from thousands of years ago, when the region was greener. The indigenous Amazigh (Berber) peoples formed kingdoms such as Numidia, whose king Massinissa allied with Rome against Carthage.

The region became part of the Roman Empire, and cities such as Timgad and Djemila flourished. Saint Augustine, one of the most influential Christian thinkers, was born in Thagaste (today Souk Ahras) and became bishop of Hippo (Annaba).

history.heading: Islamic dynasties and Ottoman Algiers
paragraphs: Arab armies brought Islam in the 7th and 8th centuries, and over time most of the population became Muslim. A series of Amazigh and Arab dynasties ruled, including the Rustamids, Fatimids, Almoravids, Almohads and Zayyanids of Tlemcen.

In the 16th century Algiers came under Ottoman protection and became a semi-autonomous regency ruled by deys. It was a major Mediterranean power whose corsairs raided shipping and coasts across the region.

history.heading: French colonisation
paragraphs: France invaded in 1830 and conquered the country over several decades, facing fierce resistance led by figures such as Emir Abdelkader. Algeria was declared part of France, and large numbers of European settlers took the best farmland, while the Muslim majority was denied equal rights.

Nationalist movements grew in the 20th century. The National Liberation Front (FLN) launched an armed uprising in 1954. The war of independence was extremely violent, with hundreds of thousands killed, and ended with the Évian Accords. Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962, and most European settlers left.

history.heading: Independent Algeria
paragraphs: The FLN established a one-party socialist state. Houari Boumediene, who took power in 1965, nationalised the oil and gas industry and pursued state-led industrialisation. Falling oil prices and unrest in the 1980s led to political opening in 1989.

When an Islamist party was poised to win elections in 1992, the army cancelled the vote, triggering a civil war (the "Black Decade") in which up to 200,000 people died. Abdelaziz Bouteflika, president from 1999, oversaw national reconciliation. Mass peaceful protests known as the Hirak forced him to resign in 2019.

culture.heading: Peoples and languages
paragraphs: Algeria's identity combines Amazigh, Arab, Islamic and Mediterranean elements, with French influence from the colonial era. Arabic and Tamazight (Berber) are both official languages, and Algerian Arabic (Darja) is the everyday language of most people. French remains widely used in business, media and higher education.
Amazigh communities include the Kabyles, Chaouis, Mozabites and Tuareg. Nearly all Algerians are Sunni Muslims.

culture.heading: Music, literature and the arts
paragraphs: Raï, a popular music genre born in Oran, became internationally famous through singers such as Khaled and Cheb Mami. Chaâbi music from Algiers and Andalusian classical music are also important traditions.

Algerian writers include Kateb Yacine, Mohammed Dib, Assia Djebar and Kamel Daoud. Albert Camus, born in French Algeria, set many works there. The film The Battle of Algiers (1966) is a classic of world cinema.

culture.heading: Food and daily life
paragraphs: Couscous, recognised by UNESCO as shared Maghreb heritage, is the national dish. Other favourites include chorba soup, chakhchoukha, merguez sausages and dates from Saharan oases, accompanied by mint tea.
Football is the most popular sport; the national team won the Africa Cup of Nations in 1990 and 2019. Yennayer, the Amazigh New Year, became a national holiday in 2018.

politics.heading: System of government
paragraphs: Algeria is a presidential republic. The president, elected for five-year terms, holds strong executive powers and appoints the prime minister. The parliament has two chambers: the elected People's National Assembly and the Council of the Nation.

The military has historically been a powerful force behind the scenes. A revised constitution was adopted in 2020 after the Hirak protest movement, but critics point to restrictions on the press, protests and political opposition.

politics.heading: Foreign relations
paragraphs: Algeria values its independence and non-alignment, rooted in its liberation struggle. It is a member of the African Union, the Arab League and OPEC, and a key gas supplier to Europe, especially Italy and Spain.

Relations with Morocco are strained, particularly over Western Sahara, where Algeria supports the Polisario Front; diplomatic ties were cut in 2021. Relations with France remain sensitive because of colonial history.

economy.heading: Oil and gas
paragraphs: Algeria is Africa's largest country by area and has large reserves of natural gas and oil, which provide the vast majority of export earnings and a large share of state revenue. The state company Sonatrach dominates the sector, and pipelines carry gas under the Mediterranean to Europe.
This dependence makes the economy vulnerable to energy price swings, as seen in the 1980s debt crisis and the 2014 oil price collapse.

economy.heading: Diversification and challenges
paragraphs: The government aims to develop agriculture, mining (including iron ore and phosphates), manufacturing, renewable energy and tourism. Generous subsidies for fuel, food and housing support living standards but weigh on public finances.
Youth unemployment, a large public sector and bureaucracy are persistent challenges. The currency is the Algerian dinar.
